hook.question: You have an $18 gift card and a shop's price list, sorted from cheapest to priciest: 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 15. Which two items cost exactly $18 together, without trying every pair?
paragraphs: Trying every pair works. Seven prices make 21 pairs. A hundred prices make 4,950 pairs, and the count grows with the square of the list.
But this list is sorted, and that is a clue. Take the cheapest item (1) and the priciest (15): together they cost 16, which is not enough. What does that tell you about the 1?
hook.aha: The 1 is out. Even next to the priciest item it falls short, so it can't be in any answer. One look throws away an item and all of its pairs. Keep checking the two ends and dropping one, and the answer turns up in a single pass: at most n - 1 checks instead of about n² / 2.

metaphor: Two friends stand at opposite ends of a bookshelf where the books are sorted from cheapest to priciest. Together they must pick two books that cost exactly your budget.
If the two books cost too little, the friend on the cheap end steps toward the middle. If they cost too much, the friend on the pricey end does.
mentalModel.click: Sorted order makes every move safe: a sum that is too small can only be fixed by a bigger left number, and a sum that is too big only by a smaller right number.

glossary.definition: An index that remembers a position in the array. You can move it, and you can read the number under it.
One pointer starts at each end and they walk toward each other until they meet. This is the pair-sum shape.
Both pointers start at the front and move forward, but at different speeds or jobs. One reads ahead, the other keeps track of what is kept.
In the same-direction shape, slow is the writer (the end of the result so far) and fast is the reader that scouts ahead.
Rule a number out for good. A pointer only moves past a number once it can't be part of any answer.
Changing the array itself, using no extra array. Same-direction pointers do this by writing over numbers they no longer need.

mentalModel.definition: Two pointers keeps two indices into an array or string and moves them by a rule, so that every step rules out possibilities instead of re-checking them. In the converging form, one pointer starts at each end of a sorted sequence and they move toward each other. In the same-direction form, a fast pointer reads ahead while a slow pointer marks where the result is written. Pointers never move backwards, so a pass takes O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

useWhen: The data is sorted (or you can sort it) and you need a pair that meets a target.
You need to compare the two ends of something, like a palindrome check.
The problem says in place, or asks you to remove, partition or merge using O(1) extra space.
Brute force would try every pair, and sorted order tells you which side to give up on.
notWhen: The array is unsorted and you need the original indices: use a hash map.
You need a contiguous stretch whose size depends on a rule (longest, shortest): that is a sliding window.
The problem is about a cycle or the middle of a linked list: that is fast and slow pointers.

quiz.problem: Given a sorted array and a target, return the positions of two numbers that add up to the target.
quiz.explanation: The array is sorted, so one pointer at each end can close in on the target. Each step drops one number that cannot be in the answer.

quiz.problem: Given an unsorted array, return the indices of two numbers that add up to a target.
quiz.explanation: Sorting would scramble the original indices you have to return. A hash map remembers each number you've seen, so one pass finds its partner.

quiz.problem: Find the longest run of consecutive days where the total sales stay under a budget (sales are never negative).
quiz.explanation: A run of consecutive days is a contiguous window whose size depends on a rule. Expand on the right, shrink on the left.

quiz.problem: Decide whether a linked list has a cycle in it, using no extra memory.
quiz.explanation: A list has no indices to compare, and the pointers need different speeds. If there is a cycle, the fast one eventually laps the slow one.

quiz.problem: Check whether a sentence reads the same forwards and backwards, ignoring punctuation and capital letters.
quiz.explanation: A palindrome means the two ends match, then the next two in, and so on. Walk a pointer in from each end and compare.

pseudocode.text: return the positions of left and right

notes: Why it never misses the answer: if the sum is too small, then left plus even the biggest number still in play falls short, so left can't be in any pair. If the sum is too big, right can't be in any pair either. Only numbers that can't be part of an answer are ever dropped.
Each step moves one pointer inward, so there are at most n - 1 steps: O(n). Only a few variables are kept, so the extra space is O(1).
The array must be sorted. If it isn't, sorting first costs O(n log n) and scrambles the original positions.
For the same-direction shape, slow marks the last number kept and fast reads ahead. Both only move forward, so that is O(n) time and O(1) space too.
LeetCode counts positions from 1, so the code returns left + 1 and right + 1, and [-1, -1] when no pair exists.

examples.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
examples.problem: Given a sorted array of integers numbers and a target, return the 1-indexed positions of the two numbers that add up to the target. Use only constant extra space.
approach: The array is sorted, so put left on the first number and right on the last.
2 + 15 = 17 is more than 9. Even the smallest number can't pair with 15, so drop 15 and move right back to 11.
2 + 11 = 13 is still more than 9, so drop 11 and move right back to 7.
2 + 7 = 9 is the target. The numbers sit at positions 1 and 2 counting from 1, so the answer is [1, 2].

examples.title: Valid Palindrome
examples.problem: Given a string s, return true if it reads the same forwards and backwards after you lowercase every letter and ignore everything that isn't a letter or a digit.
examples.input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"
approach: Put left on the first character and right on the last. The pointers will walk toward each other.
If left is on a space or a symbol, move it on. Do the same for right. Only letters and digits count.
Compare the two characters in lowercase. If they differ, the answer is false. If they match, move both pointers inward.
The pointers meet without a mismatch, so the answer is true. "amanaplanacanalpanama" reads the same both ways.

examples.title: Container With Most Water
examples.problem: Given an array height of n wall heights, pick two walls so that, with the x-axis, they hold the most water. Return that amount.
approach: Water held is the distance between the walls times the shorter wall. Start with the widest pair: walls 1 and 7, 8 apart, so 8 x 1 = 8.
The shorter wall limits the water. Moving the taller wall inward can only make the container narrower and no taller, so it can't help.
So always move the pointer on the shorter wall. Here that moves left to the wall of height 8.
Keep the best area seen. Walls 8 and 7 are 7 apart: 7 x 7 = 49. No later pair beats it, so the answer is 49.

conceptQuiz.question: The numbers under left and right add up to less than the target. Why is it safe to drop the left number for good?
options: The right pointer will make up the difference later.
Even with the biggest number still in play it falls short, so it can't be in any answer.
Small numbers are never part of an answer.
It saves memory to forget the first number.
conceptQuiz.explanation: The right number is the biggest left in play, so no other partner could do better. If left plus right is too small, left can't reach the target at all.

conceptQuiz.question: The pointers sit on the ends of [1, 3, 5, 8] and the target is 10. 1 + 8 = 9. What happens next?
conceptQuiz.explanation: 9 is below 10, so left needs a bigger number. Left moves forward to 3 and the 1 is dropped for good.

conceptQuiz.question: Why does the converging search take O(n) time and not O(n²)?
options: Each step moves a pointer inward, so there are at most n - 1 steps.
It only looks at the middle element.
conceptQuiz.explanation: Every step drops exactly one number. The pointers can only close the gap n - 1 times before they meet.

conceptQuiz.question: What goes wrong if you run converging pointers on an unsorted array?
options: It still works but takes longer.
It sorts the array as it goes.
A move can drop a number that was part of the answer, so it can miss it.
conceptQuiz.explanation: The whole argument depends on sorted order. Without it, a too-small sum doesn't tell you the left number is useless.

conceptQuiz.question: In remove-duplicates with slow and fast pointers, what does slow mark?
options: The next number fast will read.
The last unique number kept so far.
conceptQuiz.explanation: Everything up to slow is the unique prefix. When fast finds a number different from the one under slow, slow steps forward and that number is copied there.

practice.title: Reverse String
practice.insight: Swap the two ends, then move both pointers inward until they meet.

practice.title: Move Zeroes
practice.insight: It is the same-direction shape from remove-duplicates: fast reads every number and slow marks where the next non-zero belongs.

practice.title: Squares of a Sorted Array
practice.insight: The biggest square is at one of the two ends, so fill the answer from the back, taking the larger end each time.

practice.title: Boats to Save People
practice.insight: Sort the weights. The heaviest person either shares a boat with the lightest person or has to go alone.

practice.title: 3Sum
practice.insight: Sort, fix one number, then run converging pointers on the rest. Skip repeated values so you don't report the same triple twice.

practice.title: Sort Colors
practice.insight: Keep pointers for where the 0s end and where the 2s begin, and swap each number you scan into the right zone.

practice.title: 3Sum Closest
practice.insight: Like 3Sum, but remember the sum closest to the target so far and move the pointers by comparing each sum with the target.

practice.title: Trapping Rain Water
practice.insight: The water over a bar is limited by the shorter of the tallest bars on its two sides, so always move the pointer on the lower side.
